title: How the Best Performers Show Up When They Aren’t Playing
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The post proposes an overlooked test of talent: how people behave when they are not the one in the spotlight. Using a sports metaphor, it contrasts champions, who stay engaged and support teammates from the bench, with spectators who check out until called on. The author argues this off-stage behavior is a better predictor of who can be trusted with more responsibility than performance in high-visibility moments. Leaders are urged to observe people in meetings they did not lead and projects they did not get, to state the expectation explicitly to top performers, and to recognize the assist and coaching, not only the goals. The warning is that rewarding only on-stage contributions teaches best people to disengage when the spotlight moves.
points: Performance in the spotlight shows what someone can do, while behavior offstage shows who they are.
Champions on the bench stay locked in, coach teammates and keep their energy on the team goal, while spectators wait for their turn.
Leaders should deliberately observe people in meetings and projects they are not leading to judge true bench strength.
The expectation of showing up well when not playing should be named explicitly, since most high performers have never been told.
Praising only game contributions teaches stars to disengage; recognizing assists and sideline support reinforces team performance.
quotes: Top performers shine under the spotlight. They showcase their skills and talents when the pressure is on and the outcome depends on them.

Champions stay locked in and become cheerleaders for their teammates. They read the flow of the game, coach up the person in their seat, and keep their energy pointed at the team’s goal instead of their own playing time.
Anyone can look like a top performer while they drive the project or have the ball in their hands. Far fewer can look like elite performers while someone else is in charge or on stage.
That’s the harder, quieter test. It’s the one that actually predicts whether someone can be trusted with more responsibility, because it shows who they are when no one is keeping score.

Watching someone close the deal, deliver the keynote, or make the game-winning play tells a leader what they can do. Watching how they behave in the meeting they didn’t lead, the project they didn’t get, or the spotlight they didn’t share tells a leader who they really are.
They don’t just tell team members to be ready when called upon. They tell them to show up as talent even when they aren’t playing.

Recognizing off-stage excellence is also essential. When rising stars only get recognized for their game contributions, leaders teach their best people to disengage the moment they’re not in the limelight.
